newsitem.title: UK: US watchdog calls for more regulatory cooperation.
newsitem.headline: US watchdog calls for more regulatory cooperation.

text.p: Patrolling the global securities industry has improved since the collapse of British bank Barings, but more work is needed in promoting self-regulation and cooperation, a top U.S. regulator said on Tuesday.

"Much progress has been made since then, but we are still a long way off reaching the goal," Mary Schapiro, president of NASD Regulation and former Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) chairman, told an industry conference.
Schapiro said a further area of consideration was the ability of regulatory and self regulatory organisations to adapt and deal with possible changes in the market.

She also said there could be more volatility and manipulation of the market as a result of the pressures of increased competition between exchanges. Soon after the collapse of British bank Barings two years ago, regulators of the world's largest futures exchanges met at Windsor, England to discuss how to improve regulation and pool information among exchanges and markets.

Barings toppled after Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson racked up derivatives losses totalling around $1.4 billion. The dramatic decline of the centuries old bank sent shockwaves around the world's financial markets as banks, securities firms and regulators scrambled to tighten up.
Schapiro, who took part in drawing up what became known as the "Windsor Accord", said regulators still needed to work to produce responsible and co-ordinated action.
Since Windsor, there has been a two-pronged attack involving increased international co-operation between governments and improved self-regulation by markets.
There is an increasing need for self-regulation as markets grow too big to rely on government control, she added.

Schapiro said the greatest challenge facing self-regulatory authorities such as NASD (the National Association of Securities Dealers) in the U.S. was the need to keep pace with the changing market while keeping a focus on the interest of investors.
To encourage this and ensure impartiality, she said independent departments devoted to regulation needed to be set up within existing authorities.

An example of this is NASD Regulation, which she heads, an independent subsidiary of NASD. Her department has a budget of $220 million and employs 1,700 people to police the brokerage firms which make up NASD's many members, she said.
As markets grow, Schapiro said regulators will need to re-evaluate responsibilities and provide access to technological advances available in the market for regulation.
She also stressed the need to draw on the expertise and experience of market professionals who are often best placed to spot problem areas.
"It is important to devise ways to maintain and attract the interest of the leaders of industry...to secure effective regulation," she said.
And markets will need to provide new and enhanced services to keep up with screen-based trading and opportunities offered by the internet.
Schapiro said there was a need for a global perspective on regulation as the trend for foreign investment grew.
"Progress in regulation is necessary to advance common interest," Schapiro said, "Competitive considerations need not preclude regulation...provided there is adequate dialogue."
